goal: Build a reusable tool/workflow that turns one episode topic into a finished 25–35 min YouTube video: dialogue script, two separate voices, lip-synced avatar clips (Linda solo, Frank solo, both together), B-roll, subtitles, final edit.

channel.name: The Second Chapter
channel.format: Faceless AI-avatar podcast: a retired American couple debating retirement decisions on their sofa
channel.audience: Americans 60+, retired or about to retire, mostly couples, in the US
channel.promise: Two honest points of view (hers and his) on every big retirement decision, with real numbers and no sales pitch

linda.role: the optimist who organizes; makes lists; warm, quick, enthusiastic
linda.voice: bright, warm, medium pace, American female ~65
linda.look: shoulder-length gray-blonde hair, soft green knit sweater

frank.role: the careful one who does the math; dry, deadpan humor
frank.look: short white hair, light trimmed white beard, light blue button-down shirt

characters.backstory: Married couple, sold the family house at 66 after 31 years, raised three kids. Not financial advisors, not ex-police, no fake credentials.

reference_image_prompt: Photorealistic wide shot of a cozy home podcast set. A large, long beige linen three-seat sofa fills the frame horizontally. An American retired couple sits at opposite ends of the sofa with a wide empty space between them. On the far LEFT of the frame (viewer's left): Linda, 67, shoulder-length gray-blonde hair, soft green knit sweater. On the far RIGHT of the frame (viewer's right): Frank, 70, short white hair, light trimmed white beard, light blue button-down shirt. Both sit turned slightly toward each other, relaxed and natural. Each has a black podcast microphone on a boom arm in front of them. Warm living room background with bookshelves, a floor lamp, green plants, soft warm lighting, subtle bokeh. Eye-level camera, centered, 16:9, documentary photography style, realistic skin texture.

shot_library.description: Both on the sofa in the same frame, facing camera. Used ONLY for the fixed 5-8 s intro.
Close-up of Linda alone, listening (nods, small smile). No lip movement.
Close-up of Linda alone, laughing (1-3 s).
Close-up of Frank alone, listening (raises an eyebrow, half smile). No lip movement.
Close-up of Frank alone, laughing or chuckling (1-3 s).
B-roll with Linda's or Frank's voice over it.

shot_rules: Only the fixed 5-8 s intro shows Linda and Frank in the same frame; it is generated once and reused every episode.
After the intro, every clip shows one person alone: Linda's parts and Frank's parts are separate clips.
Never more than 15 s on one avatar clip; change shot every 8-15 s.
Insert a LISTENS or LAUGHS close-up of the other person between two clips of the same speaker.
Cover any glitchy avatar clip with B-roll.
All close-ups come from the same reference image (same sofa, light and clothes).

episode_structure.note: the question of the day + the promise ('number four cost us almost ten thousand dollars')

loop.mode: alternating linda_solo / frank_solo, 4-8 short lines, one joke + laugh

dialogue_style.line_length: 1–3 sentences, rarely more than 20 s in a row
rules: They call each other by name at least once per part.
Concrete numbers ('31 years', 'nine thousand dollars'), never 'a lot'.
Real disagreements; they don't always agree at the end.
Running gags: Frank's garage, Linda's lists.
Laughs are written as their own lines ('FRANK: [laughs]') or cues inside a line, 8-12 per episode, only after real jokes.
handoff_phrases: Frank, you're making that face again.
You did the math on this one, right?
Okay, I'll give you that one.
See, this is where we disagree.
If you're watching this and you're 65…
A lot of you asked us…

production_pipeline: 1. Topic → dialogue script (JSON above), 4,500–5,000 words for ~30–35 min.
2. Fact-check every number against an official source; list sources.
3. Generate audio per line with two distinct voices; assemble with 0.2–0.5 s gaps and a few soft laughs / 'mm-hmm'.
4. Split audio per line; any line > 15 s is split in two clips.
5. Lip-sync each line on the right close-up (LINDA_TALKS or FRANK_TALKS); the fixed INTRO_DUO clip is made once and reused.
6. Insert LISTENS / LAUGHS close-ups of the other person between clips of the same speaker, and laugh lines where the script puts them.
7. Generate or source B-roll for every BROLL beat (or let the Subscriber app do B-roll from the script).
8. Edit: alternate shots every 8–15 s, big high-contrast subtitles, part numbers, key numbers, 'Linda's take / Frank's take', soft low music.
9. QA: watch at 2x; no frozen shot > 15 s, no awkward silence, no unverified claim.
10. Export title, description (with AI disclosure, sources, 'not financial advice'), tags, chapters, pinned comment, thumbnail brief.
guardrails: Money, Social Security, Medicare: general information only, checked on ssa.gov / medicare.gov / irs.gov, dated, with 'This is not financial advice.'
No fake credentials or fake expertise; quote real experts by name when a topic comes from them.
Disclose AI characters in YouTube's altered/synthetic content setting and in the description.
No fear-mongering or invented 'secret rules'. Titles reuse proven formats but only true claims.
title_rule: Reuse a proven high-view title word for word and change only the niche keywords (e.g. 'I' → 'We', 'The Villages' → '55+ Communities'). Replace only words that would be false for our video.

video_method.source: Jake Trinder, 'How to Become Disgustingly Good at YouTube' (youtu.be/Dx-c19qXdxM), Oct 14 2026
video_method.principle: A video is a series system: topic, packaging (title + thumbnail), hook, body and edit must all be right; one wrong decision can sink the video.
topic: Pick topics from what the audience already chooses to watch (revealed preference), not from what we think they need.
For each topic note the floor (median views of a decent video) and the ceiling (best videos) over the last 3–6 months, 8+ min videos.
Check views look real (≈1–5 % likes per view, on-topic comments) and that demand is still active (recent videos still getting views).
Raise the ceiling by attaching the topic to a bigger demand: season, event, culture (Amish, Japanese), well-known store (Walmart, Costco, Aldi).
title: Use a title framing that wins in at least 2–3 different channels or niches, not a single outlier.
Understand why the framing works and only reuse it if that reason is true for our audience (avoid overfitting).
The title must make a promise the video fully delivers; never use false words.
thumbnail: Job 1: stand out in the feed. Job 2: be understood at a glance.
Avatar face + one object/icon that targets the audience + a tension that opens a question; the title closes only part of it.
video_method.edit: The edit matches the promise: calm and warm for our characters, useful B-roll, on-screen text for numbers, no gratuitous effects.

hook_4P.promise: Confirm in one sentence that this is what they clicked for.
hook_4P.proof: Why listen: honest proof only (sources, the character's story told as a story, a shown result). Never fake credentials or numbers.
hook_4P.plan: Announce the steps / number of items and what comes at the end.
hook_4P.persona: Name the viewer: 'if you're over 60', 'if you lost your spouse', 'wenn du einen Diesel fährst'.
hook_4P.timing: All 4 P inside the first 30–45 seconds.

body_acceptance_criteria: Decompose the title's promise: what must be true at the end for the title to be true? Break each answer down again.
That list is the outline; the script is finished only when every condition is met.
Deliver real value fast, then exceed the expectation (one bonus item, a safety tip, a worked example).
Goal is viewer satisfaction, not retention tricks.
after_publish: Early signals: positive comments per view (and what they say), likes per view, subs per view, view curve vs channel average.
A metric tells where to look, not what to change (low CTR → look at the thumbnail and ask why).
Sharp retention drop → inspect that moment (early CTA, a slow part) and cut it.
Write down one lesson per video for the next one.
pre_production_checklist: Topic has a good floor (median) and a high ceiling on videos from the last 3–6 months.
Reference views look real and demand is still active.
Topic is attached to a bigger demand when possible (season, store, culture, event).
Title framing wins in at least 2 different channels and we know why it works for our audience.
Title promise is deliverable and true, no false words.
Thumbnail: avatar face, one audience-targeting object, an open question; understood in 1 second.
Hook has the 4 P (promise, honest proof, plan, persona) in the first 45 seconds.
Script outline = the list of conditions that make the title true; every one is met.
Over-deliver: a bonus, a safety tip, a worked example.
Edit matches the promise: calm, warm, no gratuitous effects.
After 48 h and 7 days: read comments, likes/view, subs/view, retention curve; note one lesson.
